content: The genetic characteristics of HIV at the time of transmission tend to be more stable compared to those selected under the influence of antiretroviral drug pressure. Resistance-associated mutations in transmitted viruses can often be detected even years after the initial transmission event. No prospective clinical trials have definitively established whether performing drug-resistance testing prior to initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) provides a clear benefit in individuals with chronic HIV infection. However, data from several studies suggest that individuals with baseline resistance mutations may experience suboptimal virologic responses to therapy. Additionally, cost-effectiveness analyses of early genotypic resistance testing support the recommendation for baseline resistance testing in this population. Therefore, resistance testing is recommended at the time of entry into HIV care for chronically infected individuals (AII). Although no conclusive prospective data exist to favor one type of resistance testing over another, genotypic resistance testing is generally preferred in this context. This preference is due to its lower cost, faster turnaround time, ability to detect mixtures of wild-type and resistant virus, and the relative ease of interpreting the results (AIII). Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in antiretroviral-naïve individuals typically involves assessing mutations in the reverse transcriptase (RT) and protease (PR) genes. While transmission of integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI)-resistant virus is rare, the increasing use of INSTIs raises the potential for such transmission. In cases where INSTI resistance is suspected, providers may consider supplementing standard baseline genotypic resistance testing with additional testing for resistance to this drug class (CIII). Resistance assays are valuable tools for guiding treatment decisions in patients experiencing virologic failure while on ART. Several prospective studies have demonstrated that therapy changes informed by resistance testing results lead to better early virologic responses to salvage regimens compared to changes guided solely by clinical judgment. Furthermore, one observational cohort study found that performing genotypic drug-resistance testing in ART-experienced patients with detectable plasma HIV RNA was independently associated with improved survival. Consequently, resistance testing is recommended to guide the selection of active drugs when changing ART regimens due to virologic failure in individuals with HIV RNA levels >1,000 copies/mL (AI). For those with HIV RNA levels between 500 and 1,000 copies/mL, testing may be less successful but should still be considered (BII). Resistance testing is generally not recommended for individuals with plasma viral loads <500 copies/mL, as assays cannot consistently be performed at such low HIV RNA levels (AIII). Resistance testing is also useful in patients with suboptimal viral load reduction (AII). In cases of virologic failure during combination ART, resistance may be limited to a single component of the regimen. In such situations, substituting individual drugs in the failing regimen may be an option, but this approach requires further clinical validation. For patients failing their first or second ART regimen and experiencing virologic failure or suboptimal viral load reduction, genotypic resistance testing is generally preferred (AII). This preference is based on its lower cost, faster turnaround time, and greater sensitivity for detecting mixtures of wild-type and resistant virus compared to phenotypic testing. Additionally, genotypic and phenotypic assays are comparable predictors of virologic response to subsequent ART regimens. For individuals with known or suspected complex drug-resistance mutation patterns, particularly to protease inhibitors (PIs), adding phenotypic testing to genotypic testing may provide additional information (BIII). In patients failing INSTI-based regimens, testing for INSTI resistance should be performed to determine whether drugs from this class can be included in subsequent regimens (AII). Genotypic testing is preferred for this purpose. When considering the use of a CCR5 antagonist, a co-receptor tropism assay should be performed (AI). Phenotypic co-receptor tropism assays have been used in clinical practice, but a genotypic assay to predict co-receptor use is now commercially available and less expensive. Current data suggest that genotypic assays should be considered as an alternative to phenotypic assays. The same principles apply to testing for co-receptor use in patients experiencing virologic failure on a CCR5 antagonist. Resistance to CCR5 antagonists in the absence of detectable CXCR4-using virus has been reported but is uncommon. In pregnant women, the goal of ART is to maximally suppress plasma HIV RNA to optimize maternal therapy and prevent perinatal HIV transmission. Genotypic resistance testing is recommended for all pregnant women before initiating therapy (AIII) and for those entering pregnancy with detectable HIV RNA levels while on therapy (AI). Phenotypic testing may provide additional information in cases of complex drug-resistance mutation patterns, particularly to PIs (BIII). To prevent perinatal transmission optimally, ART may need to be initiated before resistance testing results are available. Once results are obtained, the ART regimen can be adjusted as needed. In cases of acute HIV infection, drug-resistance testing is recommended regardless of whether ART is initiated immediately or deferred (AII). Genotypic assays are generally preferred in this setting (AIII).
